1	# RISC-V Kernel Optimization Roadmap (Bonsai Q1_0 / Ternary Q2_0)
2	
3	Target: llama.cpp CPU backend on Andes RISC-V (AX45MPV-class, RVV 1.0, VLEN=512).
4	Baseline measured 2026-07-15 under Andes QEMU (VLEN=512, -t 8, noomp build):
5	Bonsai-4B Q1_0 ~19-21 s/token, 8B ~34-38 s/token, 27B ~124 s/token.
6	QEMU time tracks instruction count, not real latency - final numbers must come
7	from FPGA/hardware runs.
8	
9	Rules for every feature below:
10	- TDD: first add a correctness test comparing the new kernel against the
11	  matching *_generic function on random data (test-quantize-fns style),
12	  see it fail/pass, then optimize. Never commit a kernel without the test.
13	- Benchmark gate: llama-bench on QEMU (instruction-count proxy) + FPGA run
14	  (real latency) before/after. Keep per-feature commits separate.
15	
16	Status legend: TODO / IN-PROGRESS / DONE
17	
18	---
19	
20	## F0. CORRECTNESS: qwen35 (hybrid attention) produces garbage on rv64
21	
22	- Status: TODO - blocks all 27B work; fix before optimizing anything.
23	- Description: Bonsai-27B (arch qwen35, ~75% linear attention) generates
24	  incoherent text on rv64 QEMU while the same GGUF + prompt on x86 host
25	  answers correctly ("The capital of France is Paris."). Bonsai-4B/8B
26	  (plain qwen3) are coherent on rv64, and test-quantize-fns passes all 35
27	  quant types under QEMU (Q1_0/Q8_0 kernels exonerated). Suspect: the
28	  qwen35-only ops (delta-net / linear-attention recurrence, gating) in
29	  their RVV or fp16 (zvfh) paths, or a shape-dependent kernel edge case
30	  only the 27B tensor sizes hit.
31	- Evidence: scratchpad logs bonsai27b_long.log (garbage, 16 tokens, exit 0),
32	  host control run 2026-07-15 (correct, 10 t/s).
33	- Diagnosis plan:
34	  1. Rebuild rv64 with GGML_RVV=OFF (pure scalar); run 27B few tokens on
35	     QEMU. Scalar correct -> bug is in an RVV kernel; scalar also broken ->
36	     generic C op or fp16 ABI issue.
37	  2. Bisect op-level with llama-eval-callback: dump intermediate tensors
38	     host vs QEMU for one token, find first divergent op.
39	  3. Fix the kernel; add the failing case to test-backend-ops shapes.
40	- Key files:
41	  - src/models/ (qwen35 graph construction)
42	  - ggml/src/ggml-cpu/ops.cpp, vec.h (op implementations with __riscv_v/zvfh paths)
43	  - ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/riscv/ (RVV kernels)
44	- Dependencies: none. Everything 27B-related depends on this.
45	
46	---
47	
48	## F1. Q1_0 multi-row vec_dot (nrows = 2)
49	
50	- Status: TODO
51	- Description: The Q1_0 dot kernel recomputes/reloads the same activations
52	  for every weight row. Set `.nrows = 2` (later 4) so one call computes 2
53	  output elements: load + negate activations once, per row only do mask
54	  load (vlm) + vmerge + reduce. Expected ~1.5-2x on the dominant matmul path.
55	- Key files:
56	  - ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/riscv/quants.c:484-578 (vl256/vl128 kernels + dispatcher)
57	  - ggml/src/ggml-cpu/ggml-cpu.c:227-232 (.nrows field of GGML_TYPE_Q1_0)
58	- Dependencies: none. Best first step - small diff, big win.
59	
60	## F2. Q1_0 defer reductions + vector scale handling
61	
62	- Status: IN-PROGRESS (2026-07-16) - two candidate kernels implemented and
63	  verified in kernel-lab/ (q1_0.c): vl512 = per-group vl=32 + group sums
64	  packed into lanes via vslideup + vlse16 vector scales + one ordered
65	  reduction per row (zero vector->scalar moves in the block loop; correct
66	  for any VLEN >= 256); vl512w = same but vl=64 merges two groups (fewer
67	  instructions, extra slideup/slidedown data movement). All-VLEN correctness
68	  PASS. QEMU proxy on n=8192: vl256 57.5us, vl512w 64.9us, vl512 75.5us,
69	  generic 430us - see measurement note below: QEMU TCG makes vector
70	  instructions expensive and scalar ops ~free, so removing the 4 vmv.x.s +
71	  ~12 scalar float ops per block READS AS A REGRESSION under QEMU. The
72	  stall-removal benefit is only observable on vsim (rdcycle) or FPGA.
73	  Decision gate: vsim shootout vl256 vs vl512 vs vl512w before paste-back
74	  into ggml.
75	- Description: Today each 32-element group ends with vwredsum + scalar
76	  extract (vmv.x.s) + scalar fp16->fp32 + scalar FMA - the vector unit
77	  stalls 4x per block. Change to: (a) load activation scales for several
78	  blocks at once with strided load vlse16 (stride 34 = sizeof(block_q8_0)),
79	  widen once with vfwcvt; (b) collect group sums into vector lanes and do
80	  one vfmacc instead of 4 scalar FMAs; (c) unroll 2 blocks with two
81	  independent accumulator chains to hide latency. Expected ~1.3-1.5x.
82	- Key files:
83	  - ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/riscv/quants.c:500-518 (inner loop)
84	- Dependencies: independent of F1; combine after both proven.
85	
86	## F3. Q1_0 full-VLEN utilization
87	
88	- Status: IN-PROGRESS (2026-07-16) - finding from kernel-lab: because the
89	  Q8_0 activations are NOT contiguous (34-byte block stride), filling a
90	  512-bit register costs slide instructions (vl512w: 2 vslideup + 2
91	  vslidedown per block) that cancel the saved vlm/vneg/vmerge. Wider vl
92	  alone cannot win for this vec_dot shape; the width pays off only via
93	  repack (F4, contiguous interleaved rows) or multi-row amortization (F1,
94	  e.g. row A in lanes 0..31 / row B in lanes 32..63). Treat F3 as folded
95	  into F1/F4 rather than a standalone feature.
96	- Description: Kernel uses vl=32 at e8/LMUL=1, which fills only half a
97	  VLEN=512 register (VLMAX=64). Process 64 weights per step (vlm of 64
98	  mask bits) or a whole 128-weight block with e8m2. Scale application must
99	  still respect the per-32 Q8_0 groups (pair with F2's vector-scale path).
100	- Key files:
101	  - ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/riscv/quants.c:484-521
102	- Dependencies: F2 (vector scale handling makes wider vl practical).
103	
104	## F4. Q1_0 repack GEMM kernel (q1_0_Nx interleave)
105	
106	- Status: TODO
107	- Description: vec_dot is the wrong shape for matmul - it re-walks
108	  activations per output element. Add a repack path for Q1_0 like the
109	  existing q4_0_8x8: interleave 4-8 weight rows at load time, then one
110	  activation load feeds 4-8 mask+merge+accumulate chains (gemv + gemm
111	  microkernels). Largest expected win; on real hardware Q1_0 weights are
112	  tiny (1.125 bit/weight) so the kernel is activation/instruction bound -
113	  exactly what a GEMM tile fixes.
114	- Key files:
115	  - ggml/src/ggml-cpu/repack.cpp (type dispatch: ~line 4573)
116	  - ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/riscv/repack.cpp (RVV microkernels)
117	  - ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch-fallback.h:206+ (remove new symbols from fallback)
118	- Dependencies: F1-F3 learnings; biggest effort, do after quick wins land.
119	
120	## F5. Q2_0 (ternary) RISC-V RVV kernel - currently pure scalar
121	
122	- Status: TODO
123	- Description: Ternary-Bonsai models use GGML_TYPE_Q2_0 (ggml.h:432). On
124	  RISC-V it falls back to generic C (arch-fallback.h:209 aliases
125	  ggml_vec_dot_q2_0_q8_0 to the scalar version in
126	  ggml/src/ggml-cpu/quants.c:177). x86/ARM have optimized versions; RISC-V
127	  has none - a ready-made gap. Structure mirrors the Q1_0 kernel: 2-bit
128	  {-1,0,+1} weights can be handled with two masks + vmerge, or vrgather
129	  lookup. Reference the TQ2_0 RVV kernel (riscv/quants.c:6300) for a
130	  similar shape.
131	- Key files:
132	  - ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/riscv/quants.c (new kernel + dispatcher)
133	  - ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch-fallback.h:206-209 (remove q2_0 alias for riscv)
134	- Dependencies: none - independent of F1-F4.
135	
136	## F6. Andes xandesvdot variant (hardware-specific)
137	
138	- Status: TODO
139	- Description: Replace vmerge + vwredsum with the Andes vector dot-product
140	  extension (xandesvdot, listed in riscv64-linux-gcc -march=help): expand
141	  mask to +-1 int8 once, then NDS.VD4DOTS accumulates 4-way int8 dots into
142	  int32 lanes - no serial reduction until end of row. Needs
143	  -march=..._xandesvdot (gate with a CMake option + runtime/compile-time
144	  ifdef so the portable build still works). Verify the Andes QEMU decodes
145	  it before FPGA runs.
146	- Key files:
147	  - ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/riscv/quants.c (ifdef variant)
148	  - ggml/src/ggml-cpu/CMakeLists.txt:438+ (march string assembly)
149	- Dependencies: F1/F2 first (same loop restructures); Andes toolchain flags
150	  known-good (see memory: -mext-zvlsseg precedent for gated extensions).
151	
152	## F7. zicbop prefetch of next block
153	
154	- Status: TODO
155	- Description: march already includes zicbop. Add prefetch.r for the next
156	  block's qs (weights and activations) at the top of the block loop. Cheap;
157	  only measurable on hardware (QEMU ignores prefetch hints).
158	- Key files:
159	  - ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/riscv/quants.c (block loop)
160	- Dependencies: measure after F1-F3 land to avoid noise.
161	
162	---
163	
164	## Measurement setup (fixed for all features)
165	
166	- Correctness: new test vs *_generic, random tensors, tolerance 0 for
167	  integer paths / 1 ulp for float accumulation order changes.
168	- Standalone kernel lab: kernel-lab/ builds the Q1_0 kernels outside ggml
169	  (make host / make rv64 / make asm). Bit-exact vs generic + double-ref
170	  gate + --inject self-test + --bench; run under QEMU at vlen=512/256/128
171	  via run-rv64-qemu.sh. Iterate kernels here first, then paste back into
172	  ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/riscv/quants.c and re-verify with
173	  test-quantize-fns.
174	- QEMU proxy limits (measured 2026-07-16): qemu-user TCG cost is dominated
175	  by per-vector-instruction helper overhead; scalar instructions are ~free
176	  and pipeline stalls do not exist. It rewards fewer vector instructions
177	  and punishes stall-removal restructures (F2-class) even when they should
178	  win on hardware. Use QEMU only for correctness and rough instruction
179	  counts; F2/F3-class decisions need vsim rdcycle (ace-tq1 flow) or FPGA.
180	- QEMU proxy bench: ./run-rv64-qemu.sh llama-bench -m models/Bonsai-4B-Q1_0.gguf

Target: llama.cpp CPU backend on Andes RISC-V (AX45MPV-class, RVV 1.0, VLEN=512).
Baseline measured 2026-07-15 under Andes QEMU (VLEN=512, -t 8, noomp build):
Bonsai-4B Q1_0 ~19-21 s/token, 8B ~34-38 s/token, 27B ~124 s/token.
QEMU time tracks instruction count, not real latency - final numbers must come
from FPGA/hardware runs.

Rules for every feature below:
- TDD: first add a correctness test comparing the new kernel against the
  matching *_generic function on random data (test-quantize-fns style),
  see it fail/pass, then optimize. Never commit a kernel without the test.
- Benchmark gate: llama-bench on QEMU (instruction-count proxy) + FPGA run
  (real latency) before/after. Keep per-feature commits separate.

Status legend: TODO / IN-PROGRESS / DONE

---

## F0. CORRECTNESS: qwen35 (hybrid attention) produces garbage on rv64

- Status: TODO - blocks all 27B work; fix before optimizing anything.
- Description: Bonsai-27B (arch qwen35, ~75% linear attention) generates
  incoherent text on rv64 QEMU while the same GGUF + prompt on x86 host
  answers correctly ("The capital of France is Paris."). Bonsai-4B/8B
  (plain qwen3) are coherent on rv64, and test-quantize-fns passes all 35
  quant types under QEMU (Q1_0/Q8_0 kernels exonerated). Suspect: the
  qwen35-only ops (delta-net / linear-attention recurrence, gating) in
  their RVV or fp16 (zvfh) paths, or a shape-dependent kernel edge case
  only the 27B tensor sizes hit.
- Evidence: scratchpad logs bonsai27b_long.log (garbage, 16 tokens, exit 0),
  host control run 2026-07-15 (correct, 10 t/s).
- Diagnosis plan:
  1. Rebuild rv64 with GGML_RVV=OFF (pure scalar); run 27B few tokens on
     QEMU. Scalar correct -> bug is in an RVV kernel; scalar also broken ->
     generic C op or fp16 ABI issue.
  2. Bisect op-level with llama-eval-callback: dump intermediate tensors
     host vs QEMU for one token, find first divergent op.
  3. Fix the kernel; add the failing case to test-backend-ops shapes.
- Key files:
  - src/models/ (qwen35 graph construction)
  - ggml/src/ggml-cpu/ops.cpp, vec.h (op implementations with __riscv_v/zvfh paths)
  - ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/riscv/ (RVV kernels)
- Dependencies: none. Everything 27B-related depends on this.

---

## F1. Q1_0 multi-row vec_dot (nrows = 2)

- Status: TODO
- Description: The Q1_0 dot kernel recomputes/reloads the same activations
  for every weight row. Set `.nrows = 2` (later 4) so one call computes 2
  output elements: load + negate activations once, per row only do mask
  load (vlm) + vmerge + reduce. Expected ~1.5-2x on the dominant matmul path.
- Key files:
  - ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/riscv/quants.c:484-578 (vl256/vl128 kernels + dispatcher)
  - ggml/src/ggml-cpu/ggml-cpu.c:227-232 (.nrows field of GGML_TYPE_Q1_0)
- Dependencies: none. Best first step - small diff, big win.

## F2. Q1_0 defer reductions + vector scale handling

- Status: IN-PROGRESS (2026-07-16) - two candidate kernels implemented and
  verified in kernel-lab/ (q1_0.c): vl512 = per-group vl=32 + group sums
  packed into lanes via vslideup + vlse16 vector scales + one ordered
  reduction per row (zero vector->scalar moves in the block loop; correct
  for any VLEN >= 256); vl512w = same but vl=64 merges two groups (fewer
  instructions, extra slideup/slidedown data movement). All-VLEN correctness
  PASS. QEMU proxy on n=8192: vl256 57.5us, vl512w 64.9us, vl512 75.5us,
  generic 430us - see measurement note below: QEMU TCG makes vector
  instructions expensive and scalar ops ~free, so removing the 4 vmv.x.s +
  ~12 scalar float ops per block READS AS A REGRESSION under QEMU. The
  stall-removal benefit is only observable on vsim (rdcycle) or FPGA.
  Decision gate: vsim shootout vl256 vs vl512 vs vl512w before paste-back
  into ggml.
- Description: Today each 32-element group ends with vwredsum + scalar
  extract (vmv.x.s) + scalar fp16->fp32 + scalar FMA - the vector unit
  stalls 4x per block. Change to: (a) load activation scales for several
  blocks at once with strided load vlse16 (stride 34 = sizeof(block_q8_0)),
  widen once with vfwcvt; (b) collect group sums into vector lanes and do
  one vfmacc instead of 4 scalar FMAs; (c) unroll 2 blocks with two
  independent accumulator chains to hide latency. Expected ~1.3-1.5x.

- Status: IN-PROGRESS (2026-07-16) - finding from kernel-lab: because the

  512-bit register costs slide instructions (vl512w: 2 vslideup + 2

  into F1/F4 rather than a standalone feature.

# kernel-lab: standalone Q1_0 kernel verification

Extracts the Q1_0 x Q8_0 dot kernels out of ggml so one kernel can be built
and verified in isolation, without building llama.cpp.

## Files

- `q1_0.h` / `q1_0.c` - the kernels:
  - `ggml_vec_dot_q1_0_q8_0_generic` copied from `ggml/src/ggml-cpu/quants.c:127`
  - `ggml_vec_dot_q1_0_q8_0` (+ `_vl256`, `_vl128`) copied from
    `ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/riscv/quants.c:484` (`static` removed in the lab)
  - `_vl512` / `_vl512w` - new candidates developed here (roadmap F2/F3):
    group sums packed into vector lanes, vlse16 vector scales, one ordered
    reduction per row, no vector->scalar move in the block loop. `vl512`
    keeps per-group vl=32 (correct for VLEN >= 256); `vl512w` merges two
    groups at vl=64 with slideup/slidedown (needs VLEN >= 512). Reordered
    float accumulation -> judged by the double-ref gate, not bit-exactness.
  - fp16 conversion from `ggml/src/ggml-impl.h` (exact, table-free)
- `test_q1_0.c` - harness comparing every kernel vs the scalar reference

## Build and run

```
make host && ./test_q1_0_host            # x86: harness sanity (dispatcher==generic)
./test_q1_0_host --inject                # prove the harness detects a broken kernel
make rv64                                # cross build, static, RVV enabled
../run-rv64-qemu.sh $PWD/test_q1_0_rv64  # QEMU, VLEN=512 (vl256 path)
QEMU_CPU=andes-ax45mpv,vlen=256,zfh=true,zvfh=true ../run-rv64-qemu.sh $PWD/test_q1_0_rv64
QEMU_CPU=andes-ax45mpv,vlen=128,zfh=true,zvfh=true ../run-rv64-qemu.sh $PWD/test_q1_0_rv64  # vl128 path
../run-rv64-qemu.sh $PWD/test_q1_0_rv64 --bench   # per-kernel ns/row
make asm                                 # q1_0_rv64.s for LMUL/vl inspection
```

`--bench` under QEMU is NOT latency: qemu-user TCG charges a big fixed cost
per vector instruction, scalar instructions are nearly free, and pipeline
stalls do not exist. It systematically favors vl256 over the stall-free
vl512 kernels. Cycle decisions need vsim (rdcycle, see the ace-tq1 flow) or
FPGA; QEMU is for correctness.

## What "verified" means

1. **Bit-exact gate**: RVV result == scalar reference result, compared as raw
   float bits, over random + edge data (all-0/all-1 sign bits, q8 saturated
   +-127, zero scales) at sizes 128..8192. The current RVV kernels do the
   same float ops in the same order as the reference, so 0 tolerance applies
   (build uses `-ffp-contract=off` to keep both sides unfused).
2. **Double-reference gate**: |result - double_ref| / sum(|terms|) < 1e-4.
   This is the gate a future optimized kernel must pass when it reorders the
   float accumulation (per-group sums packed into vector lanes, row-level
   reduction) and bit-exactness vs the reference no longer applies. The
   per-group integer sums must still be exact.
3. **Harness self-test** (`--inject`): flip one weight sign bit, require the
   kernel result to change. A harness that passes a broken kernel is worse
   than no harness.
4. **Cross-platform checksum**: the PRNG is deterministic, so the final
   result checksum must be identical on x86 host and QEMU at every VLEN.

## Data domain constraints (match ggml, do not "fix")

- `n % 128 == 0` (QK1_0); the ggml dispatcher guarantees this.
- q8 quants in [-127, 127]: ggml Q8_0 quantization never emits -128.
  The RVV kernel's `vneg` on int8 -128 would wrap to -128 while the scalar
  reference negates in 32-bit; feeding -128 produces a false mismatch.
- No NaN/Inf scales: real quantization never produces them, and NaN payload
  propagation may differ between fp16 conversion implementations.

- **Q1_0**: pure sign bits. Smallest, no zero value. The bit layout IS an RVV mask register image, so the kernel needs no unpack at all.
- **Q2_0**: plain 2-bit fields in element order. Simple scalar unpack, but the layout is not SIMD-friendly (see 3.3).
- **TQ1_0**: 5 trits per byte, base-3 arithmetic coding. Smallest ternary format; unpack costs one multiply chain per trit plane.
- **TQ2_0**: 2 bits per trit, plane-interleaved. 22% bigger than TQ1_0, but unpack is just shift + mask; the fastest ternary format on most SIMD.

Scales: `d` is fp16 in the weight block. Q1_0 uses `d = mean(|x|)` over the block; the other three use `d = max(|x|)`.

## 2. Shared ideas

A row of K weights is stored as K/QK blocks back to back (QK = 128, 64, 256, 256). Matmul never converts weights to float. The activation row is quantized once (`from_float` to the `vec_dot_type` above), then each `vec_dot` call does integer math inside a block and multiplies by the scales only at block edges:

```
sumf = 0
for each weight block i:
    sumi = integer dot ( weight codes , int8 activations )
    sumf += sumi * (weight scale) * (activation scale)
```

The two activation formats:

```c
// Q8_0: 34 bytes, 32 elements. NOTE: 34-byte stride, so the int8 data
// of consecutive blocks is NOT contiguous in memory.
typedef struct { ggml_half d; int8_t qs[32]; } block_q8_0;

// Q8_K: 292 bytes, 256 elements, plus ready-made partial sums.
typedef struct {
    float   d;
    int8_t  qs[256];
    int16_t bsums[16];   // bsums[g] = sum of qs[16g .. 16g+15]
} block_q8_K;
```

Key structural difference for kernels:

- Q1_0/Q2_0 pair with Q8_0: the activation scale changes every 32 elements, so per-32 integer sums must be scaled **before** they can be merged (this is why the Q1_0 kernel does 4 small reductions per block).
- TQ1_0/TQ2_0 pair with Q8_K: one scale per 256 elements, so the whole block reduces to one integer, then one float multiply. `bsums` enables the offset trick in section 6.

"Plane" below means: take the same bit-field (or trit position) from every byte of a group. Interleaved formats are designed so that one plane maps to one **contiguous** run of activations - that is what makes them SIMD-friendly.

## 3. Q1_0 (binary, 1.125 bpw)

### 3.1 Packing

`quantize_row_q1_0_ref` (`ggml-quants.c:40`):

```
d = sum(|x_j|) / 128            (mean absolute value)
bit_j = (x_j >= 0) ? 1 : 0      (note: x == 0 becomes +1)
qs[j / 8] |= bit_j << (j % 8)   (LSB-first inside each byte)
```

Byte picture (byte `B` holds elements `8B .. 8B+7`):

```
bit:      7    6    5    4    3    2    1    0
element: 8B+7 8B+6 8B+5 8B+4 8B+3 8B+2 8B+1 8B+0
```

This LSB-first order is exactly how RISC-V V lays out mask registers (mask bit i = byte i/8, bit i%8). So the 16 `qs` bytes are a valid mask register image for 128 elements.

### 3.2 Unpacking in a kernel

Decode rule: `w_j = bit ? +d : -d`. There is no zero.

Scalar unpack of the codes:

```c
// s[j] in {-1, +1}
for (int j = 0; j < 128; ++j)
    s[j] = ((qs[j >> 3] >> (j & 7)) & 1) ? +1 : -1;
```

But a real kernel should not materialize the codes. Since the codes are only signs:

```
sum_j s_j * y_j  =  sum over bits set (+y_j)  +  sum over bits clear (-y_j)
                 =  2 * sum_{bit=1} y_j  -  sum_j y_j
```

The dot with Q8_0 (`ggml-cpu/quants.c:127`): one Q1_0 block covers 4 Q8_0 blocks (128 = 4 x 32). Per group k = 0..3:

```
mask   = qs[4k .. 4k+3]                (32 bits)
sumi_k = sum( bit ? +y : -y )          over the 32 int8 of Q8_0 block k
acc   += y_k.d * sumi_k                (scale per 32, cannot be hoisted)
out   += x.d * acc                     (once per 128)
```

RVV version (`arch/riscv/quants.c:484`): zero unpack work.

```
vlm.v   v0, (qs + 4k)        ; load the 4 bytes directly as a mask
vle8.v  vy, (y_k)            ; 32 int8 activations
vneg.v  vny, vy
vmerge.vvm vsel, vny, vy, v0 ; bit ? +y : -y
vwredsum -> int16            ; per-group sum, then scalar fp16 scale FMA
```

Pitfall: `vneg` of int8 -128 wraps to -128, but ggml Q8_0 never produces -128, so this is safe in ggml (documented in `kernel-lab/README.md`).

## 4. Q2_0 (2-bit, codebook {-1, 0, +1, +2}, 2.25 bpw)

### 4.1 Packing

`quantize_row_q2_0_ref` (`ggml-quants.c:74`):

```
d = max(|x_j|)
q_j = clamp( round(x_j / d) + 1 , 0, 3 )    stored in 2 bits
qs[j / 4] |= q_j << (2 * (j % 4))           (LSB-first, element order)
```

Byte picture (byte `B` holds elements `4B .. 4B+3`):

```
bits:     7 6    5 4    3 2    1 0
element: 4B+3   4B+2   4B+1   4B+0
```

The layout is **sequential**: 4 neighbor elements share one byte. There is no interleave (contrast with TQ2_0, section 7).

Precision note: with `d = max|x|`, `round(x/d)` is always in [-1, +1], so this encoder only ever emits codes 0, 1, 2 (values -1, 0, +1). Code 3 (value +2) is legal for the **decoder** and kernels must handle it (`(q - 1)` does), but the current reference encoder never writes it. Effectively the stored data is ternary with one spare code.

### 4.2 Unpacking in a kernel

```c
// s[j] in {-1, 0, +1, +2}
for (int j = 0; j < 64; ++j)
    s[j] = ((qs[j >> 2] >> ((j & 3) * 2)) & 3) - 1;
```

Dot with Q8_0 (`ggml-cpu/quants.c:177`): one Q2_0 block covers 2 Q8_0 blocks (64 = 2 x 32). Per group k = 0..1, bytes `qs[8k .. 8k+7]`, byte b pairs with `y[4b .. 4b+3]`, `sumi += (q - 1) * y`; scale structure is the same as Q1_0.

### 4.3 Why this layout is awkward for SIMD (roadmap F5)

Take a vector of the 8 group bytes and extract plane l (`>> 2l & 3`): you get elements l, l+4, l+8, ... - a **stride-4** subset of y, not a contiguous run. So an RVV kernel must pay for the mismatch on one side:

- 4 strided activation loads (`vlse8`, stride 4, offsets 0..3), one per plane; weights stay cheap; or
- expand the weight bytes in-register: `vrgather` with index `i >> 2` (each byte copied to 4 lanes), then `vsrl` by the repeating pattern {0,2,4,6} and `& 3`; activations stay contiguous; or
- repack the weights offline into a plane-interleaved order (TQ2_0-style) so shift planes line up with contiguous y.

There is no RVV Q2_0 kernel yet: `arch-fallback.h` aliases `ggml_vec_dot_q2_0_q8_0` to the scalar generic on riscv. When writing it, the TQ2_0 RVV kernel (`arch/riscv/quants.c:6382`) is the closest template, modulo this layout difference.

## 5. TQ1_0 (ternary, 5 trits per byte, 1.6875 bpw)

The dense one. A byte holds 5 ternary digits because 3^5 = 243 <= 256. That inequality is the whole trick.

### 5.1 The byte code

Encode (`ggml-quants.c:2316`), for trits `t0..t4`, each in {0,1,2} (from value + 1):

```
q    = t0*81 + t1*27 + t2*9 + t3*3 + t4     // base-3 number, 0..242, t0 most significant
byte = ceil(q * 256 / 243)                  // = (q * 256 + 242) / 243
```

So `byte / 256` is the base-3 fraction `0.t0 t1 t2 t3 t4`, rounded **up** to the next 1/256 step.

Decode one trit (plane n, n = 0 is the most significant):

```c
static const uint8_t pow3[5] = {1, 3, 9, 27, 81};

uint8_t  shifted = (uint8_t)(byte * pow3[n]); // MUST wrap mod 256 (8-bit multiply)
uint16_t t       = ((uint16_t)shifted * 3) >> 8;  // MUST be a 16-bit multiply; t in {0,1,2}
```

Meaning: multiplying the fraction by 3^n shifts n trits out to the left; the mod-256 wrap throws the integer part away and keeps the fraction. One more multiply by 3 pushes the wanted trit into bits 9:8 of the 16-bit product; `>> 8` reads it.

Worked example: t0..t4 = 2,1,0,2,1.

```
q    = 2*81 + 1*27 + 0*9 + 2*3 + 1 = 196
byte = ceil(196 * 256 / 243) = 207

n=0: 207*1  mod 256 = 207;  207*3 = 621  = 0x026D; >>8 = 2   -> t0 = 2
n=1: 207*3  mod 256 = 109;  109*3 = 327  = 0x0147; >>8 = 1   -> t1 = 1
n=2: 207*9  mod 256 =  71;   71*3 = 213  = 0x00D5; >>8 = 0   -> t2 = 0
n=3: 207*27 mod 256 = 213;  213*3 = 639  = 0x027F; >>8 = 2   -> t3 = 2
n=4: 207*81 mod 256 = 127;  127*3 = 381  = 0x017D; >>8 = 1   -> t4 = 1
```

Why rounding up is safe: the stored fraction is the true one plus an error e, 0 <= e < 1/256. After shifting by n trits the error grows to 3^n * e < 81/256. The worst case still stays below the next digit boundary exactly because 3^5 = 243 <= 256. Ceiling also guarantees e >= 0, so a digit can never come out too small. Using floor instead of ceil, or letting the pow3 multiply escape 8 bits, breaks the digits - these are the two classic bugs.

### 5.2 Block layout

```c
typedef struct {
    uint8_t qs[48];   // 240 elements, 5 per byte
    uint8_t qh[4];    // 16 elements, 4 per byte
    ggml_half d;
} block_tq1_0;        // 54 bytes for 256 elements
```

The 256 elements are split into three segments, each stored plane-major so that every plane pairs with one contiguous activation run:

```
segment A: qs[0..31], planes of 32
    plane n (multiplier 3^n)  ->  elements 32n + m,        m = byte index 0..31
    covers elements 0..159

segment B: qs[32..47], planes of 16
    plane n                   ->  elements 160 + 16n + m,  m = byte index 0..15
    covers elements 160..239

segment C: qh[0..3], planes of 4 (only 4 trits per byte, stored in the TOP
    4 trit positions: the encoder multiplies by 3 once more, so the same
    plane extraction with pow3[0..3] works; the 5th trit is a padding 0)
    plane n                   ->  elements 240 + 4n + j,   j = byte index 0..3
    covers elements 240..255
```

Byte-to-activation map used by every kernel (y = the 256 int8 of the q8_K block):

| weight bytes | multiplier | activations |
|---|---|---|
| qs[0..31] | 1 | y[0..31] |
| qs[0..31] | 3 | y[32..63] |
| qs[0..31] | 9 | y[64..95] |
| qs[0..31] | 27 | y[96..127] |
| qs[0..31] | 81 | y[128..159] |
| qs[32..47] | 1 | y[160..175] |
| qs[32..47] | 3 | y[176..191] |
| qs[32..47] | 9 | y[192..207] |
| qs[32..47] | 27 | y[208..223] |
| qs[32..47] | 81 | y[224..239] |
| qh[0..3] | 1 | y[240..243] |
| qh[0..3] | 3 | y[244..247] |
| qh[0..3] | 9 | y[248..251] |

### 5.3 Unpacking in a kernel

Full scalar unpack, in storage order:

```c
// trit(v, n) = ((uint16_t)((uint8_t)(v * pow3[n])) * 3) >> 8
int e = 0;
for (int n = 0; n < 5; ++n)                      // elements 0..159
    for (int m = 0; m < 32; ++m)
        s[e++] = trit(qs[m], n) - 1;
for (int n = 0; n < 5; ++n)                      // elements 160..239
    for (int m = 0; m < 16; ++m)
        s[e++] = trit(qs[32 + m], n) - 1;
for (int n = 0; n < 4; ++n)                      // elements 240..255
    for (int j = 0; j < 4; ++j)
        s[e++] = trit(qh[j], n) - 1;
```

Dot with Q8_K: `sum += (t - 1) * y` per element, then ONE float multiply per 256: `sumf += sum * x.d * y.d` (scalar reference: `ggml-cpu/quants.c:481`).

RVV (`arch/riscv/quants.c:6074`, vl256): the plane recipe maps 1:1 to instructions. Per plane:

```
vmul.vx   v, tq, pow3[n]     ; u8, wraps mod 256 (exactly what the format needs)
vwmulu.vx w, v, 3            ; u8 x 3 -> u16
vsrl.vi   w, w, 8            ; trit in {0,1,2}, u16 lanes
vsub / reinterpret           ; -1 -> {-1,0,1} as i16
vmul.vv against widened y, accumulate in i16 lanes
```

Segment C in RVV: broadcast the 4 `qh` bytes as one u32 (`vmv.v.x` + reinterpret), multiply by the per-lane constant vector `{1,1,1,1, 3,3,3,3, 9,9,9,9, 27,27,27,27}`, then the same `*3 >> 8`.

AVX2 (`arch/x86/quants.c:1376`) has no 8-bit multiply, so it emulates: `*3` = two adds, `*9` = shift + mask + add, and `(v*3) >> 8` via a saturating subtract plus two `avg_epu8` (lines 1400-1424). It keeps trits **unsigned** {0,1,2} so it can use `maddubs` (u8 x s8 -> i16 pairs), and fixes the missing `-1` with the bsums trick (section 6).

Accumulator width: i16 lanes are safe. Each product is at most 2*127 = 254; even after folding all planes and segments into 16 lanes the worst lane stays around 4000, far below 32767. Widen to i32 only for the final reduction.

## 6. The bsums trick (TQ1_0 and TQ2_0)

Codes are stored as unsigned t in {0,1,2} but mean t - 1. Instead of subtracting 1 per element:

```
sum_j (t_j - 1) * y_j  =  sum_j t_j * y_j  -  sum_j y_j
```

and `sum_j y_j` over the 256-block is free: it is the sum of the 16 `bsums` of the q8_K block. So a kernel may:

1. multiply raw unsigned trits by int8 activations (enables u8 x s8 instructions like AVX2 `maddubs`),
2. subtract the `bsums` once per block, before the final reduction (AVX2 does `sumi0 -= ysum` on i16 lanes: `x86/quants.c:1488-1493`).

The RVV kernels currently subtract 1 per plane instead (a `vsub` on cheap u16 lanes); both are correct. The bsums version saves one instruction per plane whenever the ISA has an unsigned-times-signed dot or when the `-1` would need an extra widening step.

The same identity is why a custom instruction (ACE-style) that unpacks trit planes should output **unsigned** {0,1,2}: the -1 folds into one bsums subtraction per 256 elements instead of hardware per-element offset handling.

## 7. TQ2_0 (ternary, 2 bits per trit, 2.0625 bpw)

### 7.1 Packing

`quantize_row_tq2_0_ref` (`ggml-quants.c:2382`):

```
d   = max(|x_j|)
t_j = round(x_j / d) + 1        in {0,1,2}; code 3 is never produced
```

Layout: two 32-byte groups, each group carries 128 elements, plane-interleaved:

```
group g = qs[32g .. 32g+31]  ->  elements 128g .. 128g+127

byte 32g+m:
    bits 1:0  ->  element 128g +  0 + m
    bits 3:2  ->  element 128g + 32 + m
    bits 5:4  ->  element 128g + 64 + m
    bits 7:6  ->  element 128g + 96 + m
```

So plane l of a group = 32 consecutive activations `y[128g + 32l .. 128g + 32l + 31]`. This is the SIMD-friendly cousin of Q2_0's layout.

### 7.2 Unpacking in a kernel

```c
int e = 0;
for (int g = 0; g < 2; ++g)
    for (int l = 0; l < 4; ++l)
        for (int m = 0; m < 32; ++m)
            s[e++] = ((qs[g*32 + m] >> (2*l)) & 3) - 1;
```

RVV (`arch/riscv/quants.c:6382`, vl256): per group, one 32-byte vector load, then 4 planes of `vsrl` + `vand 3` (+ the top plane needs no mask: `>> 6` shifts zeros in), `vsub 1`, and 4 widening `vwmacc` into i16 lanes. Per-lane bound: 4 products x 127 = 508, i16 is comfortable. One widening reduction and one `x.d * y.d` multiply per 256.

AVX2 (`x86/quants.c:1508`): same shift/mask planes, but keeps trits unsigned for `maddubs` and subtracts `bsums` once (section 6).

Kernels may assume codes are in {0,1,2} (encoder never emits 3), but the standard `& 3` after each shift already makes them robust.

## 8. Pitfalls checklist

- **TQ1_0 arithmetic widths**: the `pow3[n]` multiply MUST wrap at 8 bits; the final `* 3 >> 8` MUST be at least 16-bit. Mixing the two widths silently corrupts trits.
- **TQ1_0 encode rounding**: `ceil(q * 256 / 243)`, not floor/round. Floor makes high planes decode one too small for some codes.
- **TQ1_0 qh**: only 4 trits, pre-shifted to the top (extra `* 3` in the encoder). Extract with planes 0..3; plane 4 is a padding zero, never read it.
- **Offset**: every 2-bit/trit format stores value + 1. Subtract 1 per element, or use the bsums identity (section 6) with Q8_K.
- **Q1_0 has no zero**: 0.0 quantizes to +d. Also `vneg` on int8 assumes y != -128 (ggml Q8_0 guarantees that).
- **Q8_0 stride is 34 bytes**: activation int8 runs are contiguous only inside one 32-block. Wider vector loads across blocks need slides/gathers - this is exactly the kernel-lab F2/F3 finding; the scales can be gathered with `vlse16`, stride 34.
- **Q8_K d is float**, not fp16, and `bsums` are per 16 elements (16 x i16 = one nice vector).
- **Q2_0 vs TQ2_0 layout**: same 2-bit fields, different order. Q2_0 = element-sequential (plane = stride-4 in y), TQ2_0 = plane-interleaved (plane = contiguous 32 in y). Do not copy a TQ2_0 kernel onto Q2_0 without fixing the y indexing.
- **Q2_0 code 3 = +2 is decodable but never encoded** by the current reference quantizer; kernels must still compute `(q - 1)`, not assume ternary.

This LSB-first order is exactly how RISC-V V lays out mask registers (mask bit i = byte i/8, bit i%8). So the 16 `qs` bytes are a valid mask register image for 128 elements.

### 3.2 Unpacking in a kernel

Decode rule: `w_j = bit ? +d : -d`. There is no zero.

Scalar unpack of the codes:

```c
// s[j] in {-1, +1}
for (int j = 0; j < 128; ++j)
    s[j] = ((qs[j >> 3] >> (j & 7)) & 1) ? +1 : -1;
```

But a real kernel should not materialize the codes. Since the codes are only signs:

```
sum_j s_j * y_j  =  sum over bits set (+y_j)  +  sum over bits clear (-y_j)
                 =  2 * sum_{bit=1} y_j  -  sum_j y_j
```

The dot with Q8_0 (`ggml-cpu/quants.c:127`): one Q1_0 block covers 4 Q8_0 blocks (128 = 4 x 32). Per group k = 0..3:

```
mask   = qs[4k .. 4k+3]                (32 bits)
sumi_k = sum( bit ? +y : -y )          over the 32 int8 of Q8_0 block k
acc   += y_k.d * sumi_k                (scale per 32, cannot be hoisted)
out   += x.d * acc                     (once per 128)
```

RVV version (`arch/riscv/quants.c:484`): zero unpack work.

```
vlm.v   v0, (qs + 4k)        ; load the 4 bytes directly as a mask
vle8.v  vy, (y_k)            ; 32 int8 activations
vneg.v  vny, vy
vmerge.vvm vsel, vny, vy, v0 ; bit ? +y : -y
vwredsum -> int16            ; per-group sum, then scalar fp16 scale FMA
```

Pitfall: `vneg` of int8 -128 wraps to -128, but ggml Q8_0 never produces -128, so this is safe in ggml (documented in `kernel-lab/README.md`).

## 4. Q2_0 (2-bit, codebook {-1, 0, +1, +2}, 2.25 bpw)

### 4.1 Packing

`quantize_row_q2_0_ref` (`ggml-quants.c:74`):

```
d = max(|x_j|)
q_j = clamp( round(x_j / d) + 1 , 0, 3 )    stored in 2 bits
qs[j / 4] |= q_j << (2 * (j % 4))           (LSB-first, element order)
```

Byte picture (byte `B` holds elements `4B .. 4B+3`):

```
bits:     7 6    5 4    3 2    1 0
element: 4B+3   4B+2   4B+1   4B+0
```

The layout is **sequential**: 4 neighbor elements share one byte. There is no interleave (contrast with TQ2_0, section 7).

Precision note: with `d = max|x|`, `round(x/d)` is always in [-1, +1], so this encoder only ever emits codes 0, 1, 2 (values -1, 0, +1). Code 3 (value +2) is legal for the **decoder** and kernels must handle it (`(q - 1)` does), but the current reference encoder never writes it. Effectively the stored data is ternary with one spare code.

### 4.2 Unpacking in a kernel

```c
// s[j] in {-1, 0, +1, +2}
for (int j = 0; j < 64; ++j)
    s[j] = ((qs[j >> 2] >> ((j & 3) * 2)) & 3) - 1;
```

Dot with Q8_0 (`ggml-cpu/quants.c:177`): one Q2_0 block covers 2 Q8_0 blocks (64 = 2 x 32). Per group k = 0..1, bytes `qs[8k .. 8k+7]`, byte b pairs with `y[4b .. 4b+3]`, `sumi += (q - 1) * y`; scale structure is the same as Q1_0.

### 4.3 Why this layout is awkward for SIMD (roadmap F5)

Take a vector of the 8 group bytes and extract plane l (`>> 2l & 3`): you get elements l, l+4, l+8, ... - a **stride-4** subset of y, not a contiguous run. So an RVV kernel must pay for the mismatch on one side:

- 4 strided activation loads (`vlse8`, stride 4, offsets 0..3), one per plane; weights stay cheap; or
- expand the weight bytes in-register: `vrgather` with index `i >> 2` (each byte copied to 4 lanes), then `vsrl` by the repeating pattern {0,2,4,6} and `& 3`; activations stay contiguous; or
- repack the weights offline into a plane-interleaved order (TQ2_0-style) so shift planes line up with contiguous y.

There is no RVV Q2_0 kernel yet: `arch-fallback.h` aliases `ggml_vec_dot_q2_0_q8_0` to the scalar generic on riscv. When writing it, the TQ2_0 RVV kernel (`arch/riscv/quants.c:6382`) is the closest template, modulo this layout difference.

## 5. TQ1_0 (ternary, 5 trits per byte, 1.6875 bpw)

The dense one. A byte holds 5 ternary digits because 3^5 = 243 <= 256. That inequality is the whole trick.

### 5.1 The byte code

Encode (`ggml-quants.c:2316`), for trits `t0..t4`, each in {0,1,2} (from value + 1):

```
q    = t0*81 + t1*27 + t2*9 + t3*3 + t4     // base-3 number, 0..242, t0 most significant
byte = ceil(q * 256 / 243)                  // = (q * 256 + 242) / 243
```

So `byte / 256` is the base-3 fraction `0.t0 t1 t2 t3 t4`, rounded **up** to the next 1/256 step.

Decode one trit (plane n, n = 0 is the most significant):

```c
static const uint8_t pow3[5] = {1, 3, 9, 27, 81};

uint8_t  shifted = (uint8_t)(byte * pow3[n]); // MUST wrap mod 256 (8-bit multiply)
uint16_t t       = ((uint16_t)shifted * 3) >> 8;  // MUST be a 16-bit multiply; t in {0,1,2}
```

Meaning: multiplying the fraction by 3^n shifts n trits out to the left; the mod-256 wrap throws the integer part away and keeps the fraction. One more multiply by 3 pushes the wanted trit into bits 9:8 of the 16-bit product; `>> 8` reads it.

Worked example: t0..t4 = 2,1,0,2,1.

```
q    = 2*81 + 1*27 + 0*9 + 2*3 + 1 = 196
byte = ceil(196 * 256 / 243) = 207

n=0: 207*1  mod 256 = 207;  207*3 = 621  = 0x026D; >>8 = 2   -> t0 = 2
n=1: 207*3  mod 256 = 109;  109*3 = 327  = 0x0147; >>8 = 1   -> t1 = 1
n=2: 207*9  mod 256 =  71;   71*3 = 213  = 0x00D5; >>8 = 0   -> t2 = 0
n=3: 207*27 mod 256 = 213;  213*3 = 639  = 0x027F; >>8 = 2   -> t3 = 2
n=4: 207*81 mod 256 = 127;  127*3 = 381  = 0x017D; >>8 = 1   -> t4 = 1
```

Why rounding up is safe: the stored fraction is the true one plus an error e, 0 <= e < 1/256. After shifting by n trits the error grows to 3^n * e < 81/256. The worst case still stays below the next digit boundary exactly because 3^5 = 243 <= 256. Ceiling also guarantees e >= 0, so a digit can never come out too small. Using floor instead of ceil, or letting the pow3 multiply escape 8 bits, breaks the digits - these are the two classic bugs.

### 5.2 Block layout

```c
typedef struct {
    uint8_t qs[48];   // 240 elements, 5 per byte
    uint8_t qh[4];    // 16 elements, 4 per byte
    ggml_half d;
} block_tq1_0;        // 54 bytes for 256 elements
```

The 256 elements are split into three segments, each stored plane-major so that every plane pairs with one contiguous activation run:

```
segment A: qs[0..31], planes of 32
    plane n (multiplier 3^n)  ->  elements 32n + m,        m = byte index 0..31
    covers elements 0..159

segment B: qs[32..47], planes of 16
    plane n                   ->  elements 160 + 16n + m,  m = byte index 0..15
    covers elements 160..239

segment C: qh[0..3], planes of 4 (only 4 trits per byte, stored in the TOP
    4 trit positions: the encoder multiplies by 3 once more, so the same
    plane extraction with pow3[0..3] works; the 5th trit is a padding 0)
    plane n                   ->  elements 240 + 4n + j,   j = byte index 0..3
    covers elements 240..255
```

Byte-to-activation map used by every kernel (y = the 256 int8 of the q8_K block):

| weight bytes | multiplier | activations |
|---|---|---|
| qs[0..31] | 1 | y[0..31] |
| qs[0..31] | 3 | y[32..63] |
| qs[0..31] | 9 | y[64..95] |
| qs[0..31] | 27 | y[96..127] |
| qs[0..31] | 81 | y[128..159] |
| qs[32..47] | 1 | y[160..175] |
| qs[32..47] | 3 | y[176..191] |
| qs[32..47] | 9 | y[192..207] |
| qs[32..47] | 27 | y[208..223] |
| qs[32..47] | 81 | y[224..239] |
| qh[0..3] | 1 | y[240..243] |
| qh[0..3] | 3 | y[244..247] |
| qh[0..3] | 9 | y[248..251] |
| qh[0..3] | 27 | y[252..255] |

### 5.3 Unpacking in a kernel

Full scalar unpack, in storage order:

```c
// trit(v, n) = ((uint16_t)((uint8_t)(v * pow3[n])) * 3) >> 8
int e = 0;
for (int n = 0; n < 5; ++n)                      // elements 0..159
    for (int m = 0; m < 32; ++m)
        s[e++] = trit(qs[m], n) - 1;
for (int n = 0; n < 5; ++n)                      // elements 160..239
    for (int m = 0; m < 16; ++m)
        s[e++] = trit(qs[32 + m], n) - 1;
for (int n = 0; n < 4; ++n)                      // elements 240..255
    for (int j = 0; j < 4; ++j)
        s[e++] = trit(qh[j], n) - 1;
```

Dot with Q8_K: `sum += (t - 1) * y` per element, then ONE float multiply per 256: `sumf += sum * x.d * y.d` (scalar reference: `ggml-cpu/quants.c:481`).

RVV (`arch/riscv/quants.c:6074`, vl256): the plane recipe maps 1:1 to instructions. Per plane:

```
vmul.vx   v, tq, pow3[n]     ; u8, wraps mod 256 (exactly what the format needs)
vwmulu.vx w, v, 3            ; u8 x 3 -> u16
vsrl.vi   w, w, 8            ; trit in {0,1,2}, u16 lanes
vsub / reinterpret           ; -1 -> {-1,0,1} as i16
vmul.vv against widened y, accumulate in i16 lanes
```

Segment C in RVV: broadcast the 4 `qh` bytes as one u32 (`vmv.v.x` + reinterpret), multiply by the per-lane constant vector `{1,1,1,1, 3,3,3,3, 9,9,9,9, 27,27,27,27}`, then the same `*3 >> 8`.

AVX2 (`arch/x86/quants.c:1376`) has no 8-bit multiply, so it emulates: `*3` = two adds, `*9` = shift + mask + add, and `(v*3) >> 8` via a saturating subtract plus two `avg_epu8` (lines 1400-1424). It keeps trits **unsigned** {0,1,2} so it can use `maddubs` (u8 x s8 -> i16 pairs), and fixes the missing `-1` with the bsums trick (section 6).

Accumulator width: i16 lanes are safe. Each product is at most 2*127 = 254; even after folding all planes and segments into 16 lanes the worst lane stays around 4000, far below 32767. Widen to i32 only for the final reduction.

## 6. The bsums trick (TQ1_0 and TQ2_0)

Codes are stored as unsigned t in {0,1,2} but mean t - 1. Instead of subtracting 1 per element:

```
sum_j (t_j - 1) * y_j  =  sum_j t_j * y_j  -  sum_j y_j
```

and `sum_j y_j` over the 256-block is free: it is the sum of the 16 `bsums` of the q8_K block. So a kernel may:

1. multiply raw unsigned trits by int8 activations (enables u8 x s8 instructions like AVX2 `maddubs`),
2. subtract the `bsums` once per block, before the final reduction (AVX2 does `sumi0 -= ysum` on i16 lanes: `x86/quants.c:1488-1493`).

The RVV kernels currently subtract 1 per plane instead (a `vsub` on cheap u16 lanes); both are correct. The bsums version saves one instruction per plane whenever the ISA has an unsigned-times-signed dot or when the `-1` would need an extra widening step.

The same identity is why a custom instruction (ACE-style) that unpacks trit planes should output **unsigned** {0,1,2}: the -1 folds into one bsums subtraction per 256 elements instead of hardware per-element offset handling.

## 7. TQ2_0 (ternary, 2 bits per trit, 2.0625 bpw)

### 7.1 Packing

`quantize_row_tq2_0_ref` (`ggml-quants.c:2382`):

```
d   = max(|x_j|)
t_j = round(x_j / d) + 1        in {0,1,2}; code 3 is never produced
```

Layout: two 32-byte groups, each group carries 128 elements, plane-interleaved:

```
group g = qs[32g .. 32g+31]  ->  elements 128g .. 128g+127

byte 32g+m:
    bits 1:0  ->  element 128g +  0 + m
    bits 3:2  ->  element 128g + 32 + m
    bits 5:4  ->  element 128g + 64 + m
    bits 7:6  ->  element 128g + 96 + m
```

So plane l of a group = 32 consecutive activations `y[128g + 32l .. 128g + 32l + 31]`. This is the SIMD-friendly cousin of Q2_0's layout.

### 7.2 Unpacking in a kernel

```c
int e = 0;
for (int g = 0; g < 2; ++g)
    for (int l = 0; l < 4; ++l)
        for (int m = 0; m < 32; ++m)
            s[e++] = ((qs[g*32 + m] >> (2*l)) & 3) - 1;
```

RVV (`arch/riscv/quants.c:6382`, vl256): per group, one 32-byte vector load, then 4 planes of `vsrl` + `vand 3` (+ the top plane needs no mask: `>> 6` shifts zeros in), `vsub 1`, and 4 widening `vwmacc` into i16 lanes. Per-lane bound: 4 products x 127 = 508, i16 is comfortable. One widening reduction and one `x.d * y.d` multiply per 256.

AVX2 (`x86/quants.c:1508`): same shift/mask planes, but keeps trits unsigned for `maddubs` and subtracts `bsums` once (section 6).

Kernels may assume codes are in {0,1,2} (encoder never emits 3), but the standard `& 3` after each shift already makes them robust.

## 8. Pitfalls checklist

- **TQ1_0 arithmetic widths**: the `pow3[n]` multiply MUST wrap at 8 bits; the final `* 3 >> 8` MUST be at least 16-bit. Mixing the two widths silently corrupts trits.
- **TQ1_0 encode rounding**: `ceil(q * 256 / 243)`, not floor/round. Floor makes high planes decode one too small for some codes.
- **TQ1_0 qh**: only 4 trits, pre-shifted to the top (extra `* 3` in the encoder). Extract with planes 0..3; plane 4 is a padding zero, never read it.
- **Offset**: every 2-bit/trit format stores value + 1. Subtract 1 per element, or use the bsums identity (section 6) with Q8_K.
- **Q1_0 has no zero**: 0.0 quantizes to +d. Also `vneg` on int8 assumes y != -128 (ggml Q8_0 guarantees that).
- **Q8_0 stride is 34 bytes**: activation int8 runs are contiguous only inside one 32-block. Wider vector loads across blocks need slides/gathers - this is exactly the kernel-lab F2/F3 finding; the scales can be gathered with `vlse16`, stride 34.
- **Q8_K d is float**, not fp16, and `bsums` are per 16 elements (16 x i16 = one nice vector).
- **Q2_0 vs TQ2_0 layout**: same 2-bit fields, different order. Q2_0 = element-sequential (plane = stride-4 in y), TQ2_0 = plane-interleaved (plane = contiguous 32 in y). Do not copy a TQ2_0 kernel onto Q2_0 without fixing the y indexing.
- **Q2_0 code 3 = +2 is decodable but never encoded** by the current reference quantizer; kernels must still compute `(q - 1)`, not assume ternary.
- **Testing**: `test-quantize-fns` covers all four types end to end; for new RVV kernels use the kernel-lab gates (bit-exact vs scalar, double-reference for reordered float sums, `--inject` self-test).

## 9. Where each piece lives (quick map)

| piece | Q1_0 | Q2_0 | TQ1_0 | TQ2_0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| struct | ggml-common.h:180 | :187 | :276 | :284 |
| encoder | ggml-quants.c:40 | :74 | :2316 | :2382 |
| float decoder | ggml-quants.c:419 | :439 | :2428 | :2467 |
| scalar dot | ggml-cpu/quants.c:127 | :177 | :481 | :533 |
| RVV dot | riscv/quants.c:484 | none (falls back to scalar) | :5975/:6074/:6178 | :6300/:6382 |
| AVX2 dot | none | none | x86/quants.c:1376 | :1508 |
| NEON dot | none | none | arm/quants.c:1397 | :1574 |
| traits (vec_dot_type, nrows) | ggml-cpu.c:249 | :255 | :422 | :428 |
